job: EVAP purge valve (canister purge solenoid) replacement
unit: per job: one EVAP canister purge valve (also called the purge solenoid or purge control solenoid valve), fitted. Not included: smoke test or other diagnosis, the canister vent valve, the charcoal canister, the gas cap, and any hose or line not sold with the valve

finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so this is a first build, not a check. On the engines examined the purge valve sits on or near the intake and is a small job: every maker-stated time found is between 0.2 and 0.6 hour. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2016 Sonic about $59-$138 (0.2-0.5 hr); midsize 2019 Pilot about $59-$130 (0.2-0.5 hr); truck 2016 F-150 5.0L about $48-$145 (0.17-0.5 hr); luxury 2018 Acura RDX about $96-$146 (0.5-0.6 hr). For the Pilot and the RDX no new aftermarket valve could be verified, so the parts low is a dealer-parts discounter's price for the genuine valve ($35.29 and $35.74 against a $49.85 list; the same Honda part on both) and the parts range is narrow. The luxury example was changed from the 2018 MDX to the 2018 RDX, which uses the same valve and is covered by the same Acura bulletin, because the RDX page is the one that states both the part's condition and its fitment. These built totals sit below most benchmarks ($150-$300 is the common band), and the gap is explainable: the low ends pair an online parts price with a warranty time or a seller's 10-minute figure, which is less than a shop charges for either; shops usually bill a minimum of half an hour to an hour; benchmark parts figures are higher than the prices found (FIXD $109-$119 against $28-$65 here); and several benchmark totals include diagnosis, which this unit leaves out. A supportable site range for the valve alone on engines like these is roughly $75-$200, with $150-$300 once diagnosis is added; vehicles whose valve sits near the fuel tank, or that use a dearer assembly (the F-150 2.7L part lists at $637), will be above it. How solid the labor times are: two are maker warranty times for the example vehicle and include the maker's after-repair function test (Honda 0.5 hr for the 2019 Pilot, Acura 0.6 hr for the 2018 RDX); the 0.2 hr low for economy and midsize is Kia's time for a 2021-2024 K5 1.6T, not either example; GM prints 0.2 for the Sonic itself in two bulletins, but with no unit, so it is a cross-check only, and a further search found no maker time printed with a unit for an economy car; the truck low is a parts seller's approximate 10 minutes for the F-150 5.0L and the truck high is Honda's Ridgeline time; the 0.5 hr used for the economy high and luxury low is a named mechanic's general statement. Five of the eight labor range ends are therefore not for the example vehicle, which is why confidence is low. Sellers quote about 1 hour for older trucks (2010 F-150 4.6L, 2007-2013 Silverado V8), so older or awkward layouts can exceed the range. RepairPal's all-vehicle page would not load, so the benchmarks are mostly repair blogs. This is an estimate, never a quote and never a diagnosis. Review note (2026-11-20): Honda's bulletin 23-091 names 36162-5G0-A02 as the replacement for the Pilot valve priced here (36162-5G0-A01); both list at $49.85, so the range is unchanged.
extras: A quote usually adds diagnosis (a scan and often a smoke test; one source says shops usually charge about one hour for it), shop supplies and sales tax. The same warning light and codes can come from a loose or worn gas cap, the canister vent valve, a cracked hose or a saturated charcoal canister, and those are quoted separately; a failed canister adds several hundred dollars. Some vehicles need the valve's hose or line replaced with it, and on some the valve is sold only as an assembly with a tube or duct.
